title: Transportation barriers to voting: How Lyft is helping in 2026
summary: Voters without car access fall behind by as much as 30 percentage points when it comes to voter turnout. What Lyft is doing to help.
body_markdown:
On November 3, 2026, Americans will head to the polls for the midterm elections, but for millions of people, getting there is the hardest part. Voters without cars turn out at rates as much as[30 percentage points](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3714420#) lower than car owners. With[70 percent](https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2025/2024-presidential-election-voting-registration-tables.html) of people voting in person in the 2024 presidential election, a reliable ride to the polls matters more than ever.


#### What are the biggest barriers to voting?


In the 2022 midterms,[less than half](https://ballotpedia.org/Election_results,_2022:_Analysis_of_voter_turnout) of eligible voters cast a ballot. And, according to the[US Census Bureau](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/time-series/demo/voting-and-registration/p20-586.html) , 2.1 percent of people who didn’t vote, roughly[1.2 million](https://www.kff.org/state-health-policy-data/state-indicator/number-of-voters-and-voter-registration-in-thousands-as-a-share-of-the-voter-population/?currentTimeframe=1&sortModel=%7B%22colId%22:%22Location%22,%22sort%22:%22asc%22%7D) people, said transportation problems were the main thing that kept them from the polls.


Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey, November 2022


#### How does transportation affect voter turnout?


Most people still prefer to vote in person, which means getting to the polls can make or break turnout.[Research suggests](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3714420#) that in the 2018 general election, voters with access to a car voted at higher rates than those without one. That gap hits older voters, people with disabilities, students, and lower-income communities the most. On top of that, as many as[100,000](https://www.route-fifty.com/management/2024/03/there-are-100000-fewer-election-day-polling-places-2024/394959/) polling places have closed in recent years, making the trip even longer for many voters.


##### Mail-in voting restrictions make transportation more important


Lots of seniors, non-drivers, rural residents, part-time workers, and people with disabilities rely on mail-in ballots. But[recent changes](https://fairelectionscenter.org/postal-service-changes-and-mail-voting/) to U.S. Postal Service rules have made voting by mail harder, which makes a reliable ride on Election Day even more important.


#### What is Lyft doing to provide access to transportation to the polls


[Since 2014](https://www.fastcompany.com/91607672/need-a-lyft-to-the-polls-the-ride-hailing-app-is-once-again-offering-free-or-discounted-rides-this-election-season) , we’ve been offering free and discounted rides to the polls. Almost[4 million](https://drive.google.com/file/d/15vzMQLAlSnv7mMK-XIuvcuEl88AmM447/view) riders have used Lyft to get to a polling place, drop off their ballot, or go to a voter registration drive or related event. In fact, during the last midterms, Lyft rides to polling places were nearly 50% higher, as more voters counted on us to help them get there.


#### Where do people have to travel furthest to get to a polling place?


On average, Americans living in rural areas travel furthest to cast their vote, with an average of 5.4 miles. Close behind them are suburbanites, who traveled an average of 4.5 miles to vote. City dwellers have the shortest way to go with just 2.8 miles to their polling place.


Of course, urban planning and road design plays a part too. For some people, a closer polling place doesn’t equal convenience. However, suburbanites and rural voters take a Lyft rideshare to vote at much higher rates than city dwellers, who live the closest to the polls.


#### Do suburban voters have the longest trips to the polls?


Traveling long distances to polling places is common in suburban neighborhoods.


In some suburban counties, voters have to travel over 10 miles to cast their ballot. These are places where living and working developments are spread out over large areas, and people have little access to public transportation.


#### How do you get to the polls without a car?


If you need a ride to the polls, the good news is that you don’t have to own a car.


##### Take a discounted Lyft


To make sure transportation is more accessible on Election Day, we’re offering a special discount to the polls through our[2026 Voting Access Program](https://www.lyft.com/blog/posts/2026-voting-access-program) .*


##### How the Lyft voting ride discount works


1.


Open the Lyft app and preload the code **VOTE26** before or on Tuesday, November 3, 2026.


2.


You’ll get **50% (up to $10)** off a Lyft ride to your local polling place.


The VOTE26 code isn’t limited to Lyft rideshares. If you prefer to bike, or ride a scooter to the polls, you can use it on Lyft operated bike and scooter systems between 5 a.m. - 10 p.m. local time for the same discount.


##### Reach out to voting access organizations


If you don’t have a reliable way to get to the polls, you’re not alone. Lots of community groups and nonprofits are working hard to make sure everyone who wants to vote can. At Lyft, we’re proud to partner with these organizations to offer discounted rides:


-


[Asian and Pacific Islander American Vote (APIAVote)](https://apiavote.org/) : for discounted rides for Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders


-


[National Council on Aging](https://www.ncoa.org/) : for senior and elderly voters


-


[National Down Syndrome Society](https://ndss.org/) : for voters with disabilities


-


[Students Learn Students Vote Coalition](https://slsvcoalition.org/) : for community college and university students


-


[National Coalition for Homeless Veterans](https://nchv.org/) : for veterans experiencing homelessness


This is just a starting point. Plenty of local community groups help people get to the polls too, so it’s worth searching for resources in your area. And of course, you can always ask a friend or family member for a ride, or take public transit if it’s available near you.


#### How do I make a plan to vote in the 2026 midterms?


For millions of Americans, getting to the ballot box can be a real journey. To make it easier to vote this November, consider making a voting plan.


##### Build your voting plan


1.


**Know where to go** . Find your polling place through the[National Association of the Secretaries of State](https://www.nass.org/can-i-vote/find-your-polling-place) website.


2.


**Work with your job.**[Check the voting](https://www.onedigital.com/en-US/articles/a-state-by-state-guide-to-employee-voter-leave/) leave laws in your state. Some states require employers to give workers time to cast their ballots.


3.


**Secure your ride** . If your polling place is not walking distance from your home, and public transportation isn’t an option, make a plan for how you’ll get to your polling place. Get a ride with a friend, family member, or even a neighbor, or use the Lyft VOTE26 code to get a discounted ride to the polls.


Getting to the polls doesn’t have to be a hassle. Knowing where your polling place is and planning how you’ll get there can make Election Day a whole lot easier.


#### Voting FAQs


##### Can I use a rideshare to get to my polling place?


Yes, you can use Lyft everywhere our drivers operate. Simply open your Lyft app and request a ride. To use the VOTE26 discount code on Election Day, you can preload it onto the Lyft app any time between now and Election Day.


##### Are there free or discounted rides to vote?


Yes, Lyft offers discounted rides with our VOTE26 discount for 50 percent (up to $10) off your ride to the polls. Additionally, many communities and nonprofits provide free or discounted rides to the polls. We recommend checking with your neighborhood voting associations to find out which option works best for you.


##### What do I do if I can’t find my polling place?


Every state should have a registry of polling places, but you can visit the Secretary of State website for a[list](https://www.nass.org/can-i-vote/find-your-polling-place) of polling places in every state.


##### How can I get to the polls if I have a disability?


If you’re living with a disability you[vote by mail](https://www.eac.gov/voters/national-mail-voter-registration-form) or contact[community organizations](https://www.nonprofitvote.org/voting-with-a-disability/) in your state to find out which ones are offering rides to the polls.
